intro: If you're a homeowner in Green Bay, Appleton, or anywhere in Northeast Wisconsin thinking about a kitchen remodel, the first question is always the same: how much is this going to cost? After 10+ years of remodeling kitchens across Wisconsin, here's our honest answer — no fluff, no hidden upsells.

sections.h2: The Short Answer: Wisconsin Kitchen Remodel Costs in 2026
sections.p: A kitchen remodel in Northeast Wisconsin in 2026 typically falls into three tiers: Budget refresh ($15,000–$25,000) — paint, hardware, countertops, basic appliances. Mid-range remodel ($30,000–$60,000) — new cabinets, granite or quartz counters, tile backsplash, mid-grade appliances, flooring. Full luxury remodel ($70,000–$150,000+) — custom cabinets, premium stone counters, layout changes, high-end appliances, lighting redesign, hardwood flooring.

sections.h2: What Drives the Price Up or Down?
sections.p: Five things move your kitchen remodel cost the most: Cabinets are usually 30–40% of the total budget. Stock cabinets cost less than semi-custom, which cost less than fully custom. Countertops range from $40/sqft for basic laminate to $200+/sqft for premium quartzite. Layout changes (moving walls, plumbing, gas lines) can add $5,000–$15,000. Appliances can range from $3,000 for basic packages to $30,000+ for pro-grade. Flooring ranges from $2/sqft (laminate) to $15+/sqft (real hardwood with installation).

A few things make remodeling in Northeast Wisconsin unique. Older Green Bay homes (built pre-1960) often need electrical upgrades to meet modern code, which adds $1,500–$5,000. Wisconsin's freeze-thaw cycles mean exterior walls in older kitchens may have insulation issues that get exposed during demo. And if you're in a historic neighborhood, you may face additional permit requirements.

title: Best Deck Materials for Wisconsin's Climate (Wood vs Composite)
excerpt: Wisconsin winters are brutal on decks. Here's how to choose between pressure-treated wood, cedar, and composite — and which one actually lasts in our freeze-thaw climate.
meta_desc: Best deck materials for Wisconsin's freeze-thaw climate. Pressure-treated wood vs cedar vs composite — durability, cost, maintenance compared. Free quotes.
intro: If you're building a deck in Northeast Wisconsin, your material choice matters more here than almost anywhere else in the country. Our freeze-thaw cycles, heavy snow loads, summer humidity, and UV exposure all attack deck materials in different ways. After building hundreds of decks across Green Bay, Appleton, and the Fox Valley, here's our honest take on which materials actually last.

sections.p: Cost: $15–$25 per square foot installed. Lifespan in Wisconsin: 15–25 years with proper maintenance. Pros: Cheapest upfront. Easy to repair. Wide availability at Wisconsin lumber yards. Cons: Requires staining or sealing every 2–3 years. Will splinter and crack over time. Color fades quickly under Wisconsin UV. Best for: budget-conscious homeowners who don't mind maintenance.

Cost: $25–$40 per square foot installed. Lifespan in Wisconsin: 20–30 years. Pros: Naturally rot-resistant. Beautiful aging — silvers gracefully if left unstained. Holds stain better than pressure-treated. Lighter and easier to work with. Cons: Softer wood — dents easier. Pricier than pressure-treated. Still needs occasional sealing. Best for: homeowners who want a natural wood look and don't mind some maintenance.

sections.h2: Composite Decking: The Wisconsin Winter Winner
sections.p: Cost: $40–$70 per square foot installed (Trex, TimberTech, Azek). Lifespan in Wisconsin: 25–50 years with most brands offering 25-year warranties. Pros: Zero staining or sealing required. Won't splinter, crack, or warp. Resistant to mold and insects. Holds up to Wisconsin's freeze-thaw cycles like nothing else. Color stays vibrant for decades. Cons: Highest upfront cost. Some early composites had heat-retention issues (modern brands have fixed this). Best for: homeowners who want to build it once and forget about it.

If your budget is tight and you don't mind sealing every couple years, pressure-treated wood is fine. If you want the best of both worlds — beauty and lower maintenance — go cedar. But if you're building a deck you want to last 30+ years without thinking about it, composite is the clear winner for Wisconsin's climate. The upfront cost is higher, but over 25 years you'll save thousands in stain, sealer, and repair costs. Want a free deck estimate? Call (920) 367-1272.

title: 10 Small Bathroom Remodel Ideas for Wisconsin Homes

intro: Wisconsin has plenty of older homes with small bathrooms — especially in Green Bay's historic neighborhoods, Appleton's downtown homes, and Sheboygan's lakefront cottages. The good news: you don't need to gut a wall or move plumbing to transform a small bathroom. Here are 10 ideas that work in tight Wisconsin spaces.

sections.p: Removing an old built-in tub and replacing it with a walk-in shower can add 8–12 inches of usable space. Perfect for primary bathrooms where you don't need a tub for kids.

sections.h2: 2. Floating Vanities Free Up Floor Space
sections.p: Wall-mounted vanities make small bathrooms feel 30% larger by exposing more floor. They also make cleaning easier — no awkward corners.
Replace a swinging door with a sliding pocket door and reclaim 9–10 square feet of usable space. Especially useful in bathrooms under 50 sqft.
Vertical subway tile or stacked rectangular tile draws the eye upward, making low-ceiling Wisconsin basements and older homes feel taller.
Recessed (in-wall) medicine cabinets give you storage without sticking out into your already-limited space. We can build these custom to any size.
Built-in tile niches replace bulky corner shower caddies. Looks custom, stays clean, and adds storage right where you need it.

Paint walls in light neutrals (warm white, soft beige, pale gray) and install a large mirror — it'll bounce light and make the space feel double the size. Critical in Wisconsin where winter days are short and dark.

If you don't need vanity storage, a pedestal sink opens up the room visually. Pair with a recessed medicine cabinet for storage.
Most older Wisconsin bathrooms have one ceiling light. Add sconces beside the mirror, recessed cans in the shower, and dimmers to transform the entire feel of the room.

title: How to Choose a Reliable Contractor in Wisconsin (8 Red Flags to Avoid)
excerpt: Hiring a contractor in Wisconsin is risky if you don't know what to look for. Here are 8 red flags that will save you from a project disaster.
meta_desc: How to choose a reliable contractor in Green Bay and Northeast Wisconsin. 8 red flags to avoid, what to verify, and the right questions to ask.
intro: Hiring the wrong contractor is one of the most expensive mistakes a Wisconsin homeowner can make. We've seen it all — homeowners paying upfront for jobs that never started, projects abandoned mid-way, shoddy workmanship that costs twice as much to fix. Here are the 8 red flags that should make you walk away, no matter how cheap the quote sounds.

sections.h2: Red Flag #1: They Won't Show You a License
sections.p: In Wisconsin, contractors handling jobs over $1,000 must be licensed. Ask to see the state-issued license number and verify it on the Wisconsin DSPS website. If they refuse, walk away.

sections.h2: Red Flag #2: No Proof of Insurance
sections.p: Every legitimate contractor carries general liability and workers' compensation insurance. Ask for a certificate of insurance from their broker. If they get hurt on your property without coverage, you could be liable.

sections.h2: Red Flag #3: They Demand Large Upfront Payments
sections.p: Wisconsin law allows contractors to ask for a reasonable deposit (typically 10–30%), but anyone demanding 50%+ upfront is either undercapitalized or planning to disappear with your money.
Never start a project on a handshake. Every job — even small ones — should have a written contract listing scope, timeline, materials, payment schedule, and warranty terms.
If three quotes come in around $40,000 and one comes in at $20,000, the cheap one isn't a deal — it's a warning. Either they're missing scope, planning change orders, or cutting corners.
Ask for 3–5 references from completed Wisconsin projects in the last year. A real contractor will have plenty. Call them. Visit the work if you can.

sections.h2: Red Flag #7: They Pressure You to Decide Now
sections.p: Honest contractors give you time to think. Sales pressure tactics ("this price is only good today") are designed to skip the comparison phase.

sections.h2: Red Flag #8: They Don't Pull Permits
sections.p: If a contractor says "we don't need permits for this" — verify with your local Wisconsin building department. Contractors who skip permits skip inspections, and you're the one stuck with code violations when you sell.

title: Basement Finishing Cost in Wisconsin (2026 Pricing Guide)
excerpt: Thinking about finishing your basement in Green Bay or the Fox Valley? Here's what it actually costs in 2026, what's included, and how to budget realistically.
meta_desc: Basement finishing cost in Green Bay and Northeast Wisconsin (2026 guide). Realistic pricing, what's included, and what affects the final budget. Free quotes.
intro: Wisconsin basements offer some of the best return-on-investment of any home improvement — adding 30–50% of the construction cost back to your home value, plus years of usable living space. But the price tag varies wildly. Here's a realistic 2026 guide for Northeast Wisconsin homeowners.

sections.p: A typical 1,000 sqft basement finish in Northeast Wisconsin costs $30,000–$75,000 in 2026. Basic finishes (drywall, paint, basic flooring, lighting) start around $30 per square foot. Mid-range (better flooring, full bathroom, custom built-ins) runs $45–$60 per sqft. Luxury (theater room, wet bar, custom millwork, full kitchen) hits $75+ per sqft.

Every basement finish should include: framing, insulation (R-13 minimum for Wisconsin), drywall, electrical, lighting, flooring, doors, trim, and paint. Code-required items: egress window for any bedroom, smoke detectors, GFCI outlets in wet areas.

sections.h2: Costly Add-Ons (That Are Often Worth It)
sections.p: Bathroom: +$8,000–$18,000 depending on plumbing access. Wet bar or kitchenette: +$5,000–$15,000. Egress windows: +$2,500–$5,000 each (required for any bedroom). Waterproofing or sump pump upgrades: +$1,500–$8,000 if your basement has moisture issues. HVAC modifications: +$1,500–$4,000 to extend ductwork properly.

Older Wisconsin basements (pre-1970s) often have moisture, low ceilings (under 7'), or asbestos/lead concerns. We always inspect for these issues during the free estimate so there are no surprises mid-project. If your basement has water issues, fix those FIRST — don't finish over a wet basement.

Online calculators give you ballpark numbers but every basement is different. We offer free in-person basement assessments across Green Bay, Appleton, Oshkosh, and all of Northeast Wisconsin. Call (920) 367-1272 for your free estimate.

title: Custom Cabinets vs Stock Cabinets: Which is Right for Your Wisconsin Home?
excerpt: Custom cabinets cost 2–3x more than stock — but are they worth it? Here's an honest comparison from a Wisconsin custom cabinet maker.
meta_desc: Custom cabinets vs stock cabinets compared. Cost, quality, durability, lead times, and which is right for your Green Bay or Wisconsin home.
intro: If you're remodeling a kitchen in Northeast Wisconsin, you'll quickly hit a fork in the road: stock cabinets, semi-custom, or fully custom? The price gap is huge — and the quality gap can be even bigger. Here's the honest breakdown from a Wisconsin custom cabinet maker.

sections.h2: Stock Cabinets: Cheapest, Fastest, Most Limited
sections.p: Cost: $80–$200 per linear foot. Lead time: 1–2 weeks (often in stock). Pros: Cheapest option, immediately available at big-box stores like Menards or Home Depot, easy to install. Cons: Limited size options (only standard 3-inch increments), limited finish choices, often particle board with thin laminate, won't fit non-standard kitchen layouts. Best for: rental properties, tight budgets, or kitchens with standard dimensions.

Cost: $200–$500 per linear foot. Lead time: 4–8 weeks. Pros: More size flexibility (1-inch increments), more door styles and finishes, better-quality plywood boxes, soft-close hinges and drawer slides. Cons: Still limited to manufacturer's catalog, longer wait, more expensive than stock. Best for: most Wisconsin homeowners who want quality without going fully custom.

sections.h2: Fully Custom: Maximum Quality and Flexibility
sections.p: Cost: $500–$1,500+ per linear foot. Lead time: 6–12 weeks. Pros: ANY size, ANY style, ANY finish, premium hardwoods (oak, walnut, cherry, maple), dovetail drawers, lifetime hardware, built to your exact kitchen — including non-standard angles and built-ins. Cons: Most expensive option. Longer wait. Requires a skilled custom carpenter (this is what we do). Best for: forever homes, unusual layouts, kitchens with custom needs (oversized islands, built-in appliances, hidden storage).

sections.h2: Our Honest Take for Wisconsin Homes
sections.p: If you're staying in your home 5+ years and have a budget over $20,000 for cabinets alone, custom is almost always worth it — both for quality of life AND resale value. Wisconsin homes (especially older ones) often have non-standard wall dimensions where stock cabinets force ugly fillers; custom cabinets fit perfectly. intro: Home additions are one of the most impactful — and most expensive — projects a Green Bay homeowner can take on. Whether you're adding a master suite, sunroom, or second story, here's what it actually costs in 2026.

title: Do I Need a Permit for My Wisconsin Home Renovation? (Plain English Guide)
excerpt: Confused about Wisconsin permits? Here's a plain-English breakdown of what needs a permit, what doesn't, and why you should never skip them.
meta_desc: Wisconsin home renovation permit guide. What needs a permit, what doesn't, and why skipping them costs you more. Green Bay and Northeast Wisconsin.
keywords: do i need a permit wisconsin
intro: One of the most common questions we get from Wisconsin homeowners: "Do I really need a permit for this?" Short answer: probably yes. Here's a plain-English guide to what triggers permits in Wisconsin and why skipping them is almost always more expensive than just getting them.

sections.p: These trigger a permit in every Wisconsin municipality: structural changes (load-bearing walls), additions, decks larger than 200 sqft, electrical service upgrades, plumbing relocation, new windows or doors that change the opening size, finishing a basement, roof replacement, fence over 6 feet, and HVAC replacement.

sections.h2: Projects That Usually Don't Need Permits
sections.p: These are typically permit-free: painting, replacing flooring, installing cabinets, replacing fixtures (faucets, toilets), replacing windows in the same opening, installing countertops, and small repairs. But always check with your local Wisconsin municipality — rules vary by city.

Three reasons not to skip permits: 1. Insurance: If unpermitted work causes damage (fire from bad wiring, water damage from bad plumbing), your homeowner's insurance can deny the claim. 2. Resale: When you sell, buyers and inspectors will catch unpermitted work. You'll either lose the sale or have to fix it retroactively at 3x the cost. 3. Safety: Inspections catch mistakes that could cause real harm — fires, collapses, gas leaks.

title: Can You Build in Winter in Wisconsin? 5 Myths Debunked
excerpt: Most Wisconsin homeowners think construction stops in winter. Here's why that's wrong — and why winter can actually be a great time to remodel.
meta_desc: Can you build or remodel in winter in Wisconsin? 5 myths debunked. Why winter remodeling can actually be cheaper and faster than summer projects.
intro: Most Wisconsin homeowners assume construction grinds to a halt November through March. The truth is more nuanced — and often, winter is actually a GREAT time to remodel. Here are 5 winter construction myths we hear all the time.

sections.h2: Myth #1: Contractors Don't Work in Winter
sections.p: Reality: Most legitimate Wisconsin contractors work year-round. Interior work — kitchens, bathrooms, basements, custom carpentry, renovations — happens all winter long. We're busiest in summer, so winter is actually when we can give projects more focused attention.

sections.h2: Myth #2: Winter Construction is More Expensive
sections.p: Reality: The opposite is often true. Material costs are usually lower in winter (off-peak), and contractors with winter availability often offer better pricing because demand is lower. The exception: foundation work or major exterior projects.

Reality: Interior projects often go FASTER in winter because there are fewer parallel projects pulling on subcontractors (electricians, plumbers). Material delivery is also faster when supply chains aren't strained by summer demand.

Reality: Modern materials (paint, drywall mud, adhesives) are formulated to work at indoor temperatures year-round. Wood acclimates fine in heated indoor spaces. The only concern is exterior work like concrete and roofing, which we schedule for spring or fall.

sections.h2: Myth #5: Permits Take Forever in Winter
sections.p: Reality: Wisconsin building departments are LESS busy in winter, so permits often come back faster. Inspections are typically scheduled within 2–5 days instead of the 1–2 week summer wait.

Kitchen remodels, bathroom remodels, basement finishing, custom carpentry, interior painting, flooring replacement, drywall work, and built-in cabinetry are all perfect winter projects. Want to start your winter remodel? Call (920) 367-1272.
